html:
The gold coin issued by the caliph Abd al-Malik in 696 to 697 (year 77 of the Islamic calendar), bearing only Arabic writing: the Muslim declaration of faith and verses of the Quran, with no pictures at all. It became one of the most trusted coins of the medieval world.

Before this, the caliphate used coins copied from the gold solidus of the Byzantine Empire and the silver of the Sasanian Empire, with emperors, crosses and fire altars. Abd al-Malik's reform, together with his switch to Arabic for government records and his Dome of the Rock, gave the empire a clear Islamic identity. A silver dirham of the same style followed in 698.

The name dinar comes from the Roman denarius. The coin held a steady weight of gold, about 4.25 grams, and passed in trade from Spain to India. Even the English king Offa of Mercia struck a gold coin copying a later dinar, Arabic writing and all. The Abbasid caliphs kept the design, and the word dinar is still the name of money in several countries.
